name: Law of Triviality
description: Groups can spend disproportionate time debating small, easy-to-grasp details while under-discussing the harder, more consequential architecture behind them. In software and product work, this is usually called bikeshedding.
design_relevance_note: Directly relevant to critique, roadmap, and design-review practice: teams may burn cycles on icon shade, copy wording, or button radius because those details are easier to discuss than the underlying information architecture, policy, or system constraints.
myth_risk_note: No rigorous peer-reviewed empirical backing exists for Law of Triviality as a validated organizational bias -- it originated and remains a management-book/software-culture aphorism, not an empirically tested phenomenon, despite being widely cited as if it were established science.
prevalence_note: The alias 'bikeshedding' is common across software, product, and design-review culture, even though the formal phrase 'Law of Triviality' is used less often.

applications.title: Poul-Henning Kamp's 1999 FreeBSD 'bikeshed' email
applications.description: After a lengthy freebsd-hackers mailing-list argument over whether the sleep(1) command should accept fractional-second arguments -- a small, easy-to-have-an-opinion-about detail -- FreeBSD developer Poul-Henning Kamp posted a message titled 'A bike shed (any colour will do) on greener grass...' explicitly invoking Parkinson's law of triviality (via the 1957 bikeshed/atomic-plant anecdote) to explain why the group was spending disproportionate energy on the trivial detail while harder, more consequential design questions went undiscussed.
applications.ethical_note: This is a pure internal-process/productivity illustration with no persuasion, dark-pattern, or user-facing dimension at all -- a mailing-list dispute about a command-line argument, not a design decision that touches an end user. Included because it's the single strongest real, named, dated instance of the Law of Triviality's own dynamic actually playing out (a technical team burning disproportionate attention on the easy-to-argue-about detail), which is exactly what this corpus's 'Popular but Unverified' cell needs: a real misapplication example for a heuristic that has no rigorous empirical backing of its own.
